hints: Start with what specificity really means: only one shape of substrate fits into the active site, so ask yourself which level of structure creates that exact 3D shape.

Remember how the levels build on each other in 9700: primary sequence determines hydrogen bonding for secondary, which folds into tertiary, which arranges subunits in quaternary, so a change at a lower level can reshape everything above it.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes an enzyme specific**

Think of specificity as lock and key. It is the precise 3D shape and chemistry of the active site that lets only one substrate fit.

That shape is not made in isolation, it is built up from all the folding levels below it.

**Link primary and secondary to the active site**

Primary structure (1) is the sequence of amino acids. This determines where R groups are, so it determines where hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and disulfide bridges can form.

Secondary structure (2), the alpha helices and beta pleated sheets, starts the folding that brings distant amino acids together to form the active site pocket.

**Add tertiary and quaternary and conclude**

Tertiary structure (3) is the final 3D folding of one polypeptide. This directly creates the shape of the active site for most enzymes.

Quaternary structure (4) is the arrangement of multiple polypeptides. For an enzyme with more than one subunit, this arrangement can also shape or influence the active site. Since 1 determines 2, which determines 3, which determines 4, all four levels can determine specificity.

options.A: Correct and well done for seeing the whole chain. Primary determines secondary and tertiary folding, and quaternary arrangement, so all four can affect active site shape and specificity.
options.B: Close, but incomplete. It correctly includes 1, 2 and 3 but wrongly leaves out quaternary, which matters when an enzyme is made of two or more polypeptides.
options.C: Not quite. It wrongly leaves out tertiary (3), yet tertiary folding is what directly forms the 3D active site in a single polypeptide.
options.D: This is the common trap. Tertiary and quaternary do shape the active site directly, but primary and secondary determine that folding, so they also determine specificity.
